If differences in species richness across tetrapod clades are driven primarily by variation in evolutionary time (time-for-speciation) rather than by contemporary climate or speciation rates, then structural equation models should show stronger direct positive effects of assemblage age on species richness compared to the direct effects of temperature, precipitation, productivity, or speciation rates across the majority of clades, with this pattern being more pronounced in older and more widespread clades.

If species richness in terrestrial tetrapod clades is jointly determined by evolutionary time for diversification to occur, the rate at which lineages speciate, and contemporary climate-mediated productivity, then the relative importance of these factors as direct and indirect drivers of richness should vary predictably across clades according to their intrinsic biological traits such as thermal physiology and extrinsic geographic attributes such as spatial extent, rather than conforming to a single universal model of diversity regulation.

Species richness in terrestrial tetrapod clades is jointly determined by evolutionary time (species accumulation through prolonged in situ persistence) and speciation rates (diversification dynamics), with the relative importance of these pathways and their mediation by climate and productivity varying predictably across clades based on thermal physiology, clade age, and geographic extent, such that older, more widespread endothermic clades show stronger historical legacy effects while younger, more restricted ectothermic clades show stronger cradle-of-diversity effects mediated by climate-driven speciation.
